title: You Need to Work on Your Pace
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: This article by Mr. Nickhart challenges the common lesson observation feedback 'you need to work on your pace,' arguing that pace is almost never the real variable in play and that feedback of this kind reveals structural weaknesses in how school leaders understand and conduct observations. The author inventories the assumptions embedded in pace feedback — that faster is better, that the observer's own processing speed is a valid proxy for students', that the fastest learners should set the rhythm — and finds all of them empirically questionable. Pace, properly understood, is a downstream symptom: what looks like a pace problem is almost always a curriculum issue (task design, scaffolding, modelling, sequencing) invisible to an observer watching a single lesson snapshot. The article argues that two structural conditions are required for lesson observation feedback to be genuinely useful at all: a shared, evidence-informed pedagogical framework that gives observers a principled vocabulary, and joint observations pairing non-specialists with subject experts who can see past surface features. Without both, even well-intentioned feedback defaults to the superficial — and 'work on your pace' is the archetypal example of superficial feedback that burdens teachers with solving the wrong problem.
points: Pace feedback encodes at least seven distinct observer assumptions simultaneously — that faster is better, that the teacher is responsible for differentiated challenge, that the observer's adult processing speed predicts student processing speed — and none of these assumptions survive scrutiny as the highest-leverage variable in learning.

What appears as a pace problem in a lesson observation is almost always an upstream curriculum issue: task design pitched too low, scaffolding insufficiently faded, or connections not built into task structure — problems that speeding up instruction cannot fix and may actively worsen.

A shared pedagogical framework is not about mandating strategies but about giving observers an evidence-informed mental model against which to interpret what they see, preventing defaulting to superficial proxies like pace when more fundamental instructional variables are at play.

Non-specialist observers are structurally incapable of providing high-leverage feedback because they can only notice surface features and student reactions — which means meaningful lesson observation requires pairing SLT non-specialists with age- and subject-specialist observers for every session.

Pace feedback is only valid under a very narrow and rarely-met condition: all students have fully grasped appropriately-pitched content and are genuinely under-challenged — a situation that rarely obtains and that, when it does, points to task design as the fix, not speed.
quotes: I've heard this feedback given directly (to me, many years ago) and to others over the years. I've also heard it anecdotally from teachers recounting how their lesson observation went. And I think it represents a problem with lesson observations.
The observer assumes that their own processing speed (as an educated adult) is a reliable proxy for students' processing speed.
A pedagogical framework can be principle led, helping leaders to hold an evidence informed mental model of what makes great teaching to help make sense of what they are seeing in lesson observations.
A non specialist tasked with observing and feeding back can at best notice superficial features of practice or students' reactions to the flow of a lesson.

Going faster is unlikely to change the conditions required for learning to be more effective. Children need fluency practice, which could look like the lesson is going slower. They need opportunities to recall prior knowledge and make connections; going faster only benefits the students who do this quickest.

A teacher trying to act on the feedback of increasing pace without considering task design, modelling, scaffolding etc will likely experience frustration. Better designed examples for modelling might enable quicker grasping of content. Better faded scaffolding might enable students to more quickly internalise processes.

I think that what looks like a pace problem is almost certainly something else upstream. Furthermore and more importantly, if pace is the feedback of lesson observations, I'd argue more work needs to be done on the concept of lesson observations and their developmental and evaluative use among the leadership team.
